title: Communication and customer service skills
monthTitle: The Helpdesk Professional: ITIL, Ticketing & Soft Skills
summary: Master the communication and customer-service skills that turn a technically correct fix into a genuinely good support experience, including how to handle difficult users.
objectives: Open and close a support interaction professionally
Use active listening and confirm understanding before acting
Explain technical things to non-technical users without jargon
Apply techniques to de-escalate a frustrated or angry user
Set expectations clearly and keep users informed
Maintain professionalism, empathy, and proper phone/written etiquette

quiz.q: What is 'active listening' on a support call?
options: Fully focusing, not interrupting, and confirming you understood
Reading from a script word for word
quiz.why: Active listening means concentrating on the user, letting them finish, and restating the issue to confirm you understood before you start fixing.

quiz.q: A user is angry about repeated outages. What is the best first response?
options: Acknowledge their frustration and apologise for the impact, then focus on helping
quiz.why: Acknowledging feelings and the impact de-escalates; arguing, dismissing, or blaming others escalates. Empathy first, then action.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid technical jargon with most users?
options: It confuses and alienates non-technical users and slows resolution
quiz.why: Plain language keeps the user with you, reduces confusion and repeat questions, and makes them feel respected rather than talked down to.

quiz.q: What does 'setting expectations' mean in support?
options: Clearly telling the user what will happen next and roughly when
quiz.why: Setting expectations means telling the user the next step and timeframe so they are not left wondering; under-promise and over-deliver.

quiz.q: Give one phrase you can use to show empathy to a frustrated user, and explain why it works.
quiz.answer: Something like 'I completely understand how disruptive this is, and I'm going to help you get it sorted.' It works because it acknowledges their feelings and signals you are on their side.
quiz.why: Empathy phrases validate the user's experience and shift the conversation from conflict to collaboration.

quiz.q: Why is it important to confirm the user's issue back to them before troubleshooting?
quiz.answer: Restating the issue confirms you understood it correctly, catches misunderstandings early, and reassures the user you were listening.
quiz.why: Confirming understanding prevents you from solving the wrong problem and builds trust at the start of the interaction.

body_markdown:
## The fix is only half the job

A technically perfect resolution delivered rudely is a *bad* support experience. Users remember how you made them feel as much as whether the problem went away. **Communication** and **customer service** are not soft extras on a helpdesk — they are the core of the job. This lesson gives you concrete techniques you can use on your very next call.

## Open and close professionally

Every interaction has a shape. Open warmly, identify yourself, and confirm who you are helping. Close by confirming resolution and inviting follow-up.

```text
Opening:
"Good morning, IT Service Desk, this is Daniel. How can I help today?"

Closing:
"Great, your email is working now. I'll keep the ticket open
until end of day in case anything recurs. Anything else I can help with?"
```

A clear open and close makes you sound calm and in control even when the middle is messy.

## Listen actively and confirm understanding

**Active listening** means giving the user your full attention, letting them finish, and then **restating** the issue in your own words. This catches misunderstandings before you waste time solving the wrong thing.

```text
"So just to confirm - your laptop connects to Wi-Fi at home,
but not in the office since this morning. Is that right?"
```

That one sentence reassures the user you were listening and locks in a shared understanding.

## Drop the jargon

Most users are not technical. Translate. Instead of "your DNS resolver is misconfigured," say "your computer is looking up website addresses in the wrong place — I'll point it to the right one." Plain language respects the user and keeps them with you. Never make someone feel stupid for not knowing IT — that is *your* job, not theirs.

## Set expectations and keep people informed

Uncertainty is what frustrates users most. Always tell them **what happens next and roughly when**. Under-promise and over-deliver.

```text
"This one needs our network team. I'm escalating it now with
all your details. You should hear back within two hours, and
I've put my notes on the ticket so you won't repeat yourself."
```

If you say you will call back, call back — even if it is only to say there is no news yet.

## De-escalating a frustrated user

Angry users are usually frustrated by the *situation*, not by you. Do not take it personally, and never argue or blame other teams. Lead with **empathy**, then move to **action**.

```text
User: "This is the third time this week! It's unacceptable."
You:  "You're right, and I'm sorry - that's genuinely disruptive.
       Let's get you working now, and I'll flag the repeat issue
       so it gets properly investigated."
```

Acknowledge the feeling, take ownership of the next step, and stay calm. Tone of voice matters as much as words.

## Your task

Write a short script for this call: a user phones, clearly stressed, because their presentation file won't open thirty minutes before a big client meeting. Write your opening line, one empathy statement, one sentence confirming the issue back to them, and a closing line that sets expectations. Keep every line jargon-free.

bullets: Uncertainty frustrates users most.

slides.narration: One of the biggest sources of frustration is uncertainty. So always set expectations: tell the user what happens next and roughly when. Under-promise and over-deliver. The example here escalates the ticket, gives a realistic timeframe, and reassures the user they won't have to repeat themselves. And a golden rule: if you say you'll call back, call back, even if it's only to say there's no news yet. Reliability builds trust faster than anything else.

bullets: Anger is at the situation, not you.

slides.narration: Sometimes a user is angry. Remember, they're almost always frustrated by the situation, not by you personally, so don't take it to heart, and never argue or blame other teams. The technique is simple: lead with empathy, then move to action. In the example, you agree with them, apologise for the disruption, then immediately pivot to helping. Acknowledge the feeling, own the next step, and stay calm. Your tone of voice carries as much weight as your actual words.

slides.title: Empathy in writing too
bullets: The same skills apply to email and chat.
Read your message before you send it.
Warm, clear, and free of jargon.
Avoid blunt one-word replies.
slides.narration: Everything we've covered applies to written support too, in email and chat, where you don't have tone of voice to soften things. So read your message back before you send it. Is it warm, clear, and free of jargon? A blunt one-word reply can feel cold or dismissive even when you didn't mean it that way. A little extra care in writing, a friendly greeting, a clear explanation, a polite close, goes a long way when the user can't hear your voice.
